entries.title: Chicago Snowballs cancel opening weekend games because of setbacks due to severe weather
entries.summary: <p>Opening weekend baseball games for the Chicago Snowballs, the city’s newest co-ed baseball team offering a style of play popularized by the Savannah Bananas, have been canceled.</p><p>The two games, scheduled for May 2 and 3 at Kerry Wood Cubs Field in Roscoe Village, were called off due to severe weather in recent days that caused the team to miss practice time. Problems with the functionality of the ballpark's scoreboard was also an issue, said Snowballs CEO Cherie Travis.</p><p>The thousand or so fans who had tickets to each of the sold-out games are being offered tickets to future games, including the next game in the Chicago area, scheduled for May 29 at 6:30 p.m. at Wintrust Field in Schaumburg.</p><p>"We're basically offering people tickets to any other game they want to come to, and if they go to games being held at bigger ballparks, like the ones in Schaumburg, Crestwood, Geneva or Joliet, we're offering two extra free tickets," Travis said. "And, obviously, anyone who just wants a refund, we will give it to them."</p><p>Members of her staff have been texting, calling and emailing ticket holders to share news of the cancellations. A few fans were initially suspicious of a phishing scam, and though there was disappointment, most said they were still excited to get to an upcoming game, Travis said.</p><p>"We've been trying to accommodate people as best we can, but everyone in Chicago knows we've had terrible weather," Travis said.</p><p>"My entertainment director reminded me that sometimes even Broadway shows get pushed back," she said. "But we've been working really hard and we're just so excited to bring our baseball circus, with so many different forms of entertainment, from baseball trick plays to singing and dancing and tumbling and juggling, to the people."</p><p>The Snowballs will compete against another team that Travis just formed — the Rocket Squirrels, the crafty, sneaky, mischievous prankster little brother counterpart to the jolly Snowballs.<br></p>

entries.title: First-rounder Dillon needs to be a thrillin’ fill-in
entries.summary: <p>To Edge or not to Edge?</p><p>To Safety first?</p><p>To “need” or to “fit”? Or to do neither and “best available” the whole thing and make all plans work from there? Because, recently, that seemed to be the Chef Poles Michelin-starred recipe.</p><p>The talk as it led up to Thursday’s Day 1 in the 2026 NFL Draft got louder and louder about Oregon’s Dillon Thieneman or Toledo’s Emmanuel McNeil-Warren being one of the dudes general manager Ryan Poles was going to pull the plug on when it came to the 25th pick. That one of them was going to be his guy, the one he trusts to be his “next best” find. The defensive equivalent of Luther Burden III, if you will. That kind of discovery.</p><p>But rumor had it that the Vikings had all eyes on Thieneman to be the sequel to their six-time All-Pro, 14-year safety Harrison Smith. Literally. Figuratively. Prototypically. Positionally. Racially. Draft-wise.</p><p>So the Bears had to look at other voids to fill with their first pick.</p><p>Other player’s names surfaced. Kadyn Proctor (OT), the wish. T.J. Parker (Edge), the gamble. Caleb Lomu (OT), the coulda. Dani Dennis-Sutton (Edge), the wild card. All parts of someone’s mock draft leading up to the Bears’ pick. Know that “mock” in many of these cases is short for “mockery.”</p><p>For the first time in four years, Chicago didn’t have a selection in the top 10 of the draft. This time they had a first-round pick that Marcus Spears or Mel Kiper Jr. didn’t talk a lot about. The last time the Bears drafted in the 20s of the first round was 2013, where at No. 20 they selected Kyle Long, who turned out to be a three-time Pro Bowl player while with the Bears.</p><p>Could it happen again?</p><p>History never really repeats itself, it just sequels. Sometimes in mysterious ways. Being on the clock that deep in the no man’s land of the first round can be either meaningless or meaningful. The Vikings flipped their own script on themselves. Drafting D-lineman Caleb Banks. So to make it meaningful, Thieneman got the Bears’ Day 1 call.</p><p>The Bears spoke of “silent tape” players who they were in search of. Players with “that dog in them” is what they sought. We won’t know until later whether Thieneman, Iowa center Logan Jones, Stanford tight end Sam Roush and LSU receiver Zavion Thomas are those finds.</p><p>Assistant GM Jeff King said as he sat in for Poles during the pre-draft presser before the draft: “As we head into this weekend, we’re prepared. We’ll be adaptable. We’ll make the best decisions for the team today and going forward. The goal by the end of the weekend is to add talent, competition, bring the right football players and the right character into the building.” The type of generalized scripted words ESPN football analyst Joey Galloway would probably counter with a “You don’t know [who you drafted] ’til a guy shows up.”</p><p>Shows up at your facility’s doorstep. In film study. On the field. In pads. When the ref blows the whistle. When a contract extension is on the line. Making this year’s selections — by placement alone on Days 1 and 2 — more of a gamble than any the Bears have made in recent memory.</p><p>For the Bears, it all came down to this as primary: How do you replace loss? Loss that comes with the cost of winning. How do you fill voids un-fillable in the moment when you need voids filled at that very moment? Kevin Byard III, Nahshon Wright, C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Jaquan Brisker, all gone. Not saying a rookie at any secondary position (safety, corner or nickel) is going replace any of those single losses let alone all four, but with the Bears last season leading the NFL in passing touchdowns allowed over 20 yards and second in the league in giving up any completions over 20 yards (but they did lead the NFL in takeaways and interceptions, so there’s that), you gotta start somewhere, right?</p><p>No pressure on Thieneman but his comps won’t be just Smith or Long — or John Lynch or Eric Weddle or Bears legends Gary Fencik or Doug Plank. Not for a team whose drop in first-round draft positioning is directly related to their suddenly achievable Super Bowl aspirations. Stakes is high surrounding all Halas Hall moves now. Even with a safety as a 25th pick in the draft.</p><p><i>And with the 24th pick of the 2002 NFL Draft, the Baltimore Ravens select, Ed Reed.</i></p><p>A sequel?<br></p>

entries.title: Caleb Thielbar the latest Cubs pitcher to head to the injured list
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — If you’ve seen “Sinners,” you were reminded what it takes to get rid of vampires.</p><p>Nicky Lopez is no vampire, but it’s clear that when it comes to how many lives he has with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs,</a> no one has driven a stake through his heart just yet.</p><p>“It feels unbelievable,’’ said the Naperville-raised Lopez, who was acquired — again — by the Cubs from Colorado, where he was playing in Triple-A Albuquerque for the Rockies and joined the big club Friday night.</p><p>“It feels like the first, second, third time I was with the team, a dream come true,’’ Lopez said. “It always is, to be able to put that jersey on. And I told you guys, like my grandpa is a die-hard Cubs fan, and he’s still with us, obviously.</p><p>“So whenever I can put a Cubs jersey on, it always makes me ride through him and the family, he said. Just again, to get that call from the Cubs — ‘Are you interested?’ It was a no-brainer.”</p><p>Lopez’s acquisition was one of a flurry of moves made by the Cubs, whose president of baseball operations, Jed Hoyer, is traveling with the club.</p><p>Lopez takes the roster spot of infielder Scott Kingery, who was designated for assignment two days after making two throwing errors at third base.</p><p>The Cubs’ ravaged bullpen took another significant hit when left-hander Caleb Thielbar, who had been filling in as the closer while Daniel Palencia works his way back from an oblique strain, went on the 15-day injured list. His roster spot was filled by well-traveled Vince Velasquez, the 33-year-old right-hander whom the Cubs signed this past offseason to a minor-league deal with a spring-training invite.</p><p>“It looks like it’s on the mild side,’’ manager Craig Counsell told reporters in addressing Thielbar’s injury. “He had a similar injury in 2022, and this looks like a less serious version. We’re hoping that he’ll be out fairly close to the minimum.’’</p><p>Velazquez’s 17 innings leads the Iowa Cubs. He has a 1-0 record with a 3.71 ERA.</p><p>Thielbar left Thursday’s extra-inning win over the Phillies in obvious discomfort. He had made 11 appearances for the Cubs, recording two wins and two saves.</p><p>To create a spot for Velasquez, the Cubs transferred reliever Porter Hodge, who is recovering from Tommy John elbow surgery, to the 60-day injured list.</p><p>Going back to spring training, the Cubs have lost pitchers Shelby Miller, Jordan Wicks, Hodge, Cade Horton, Phil Maton, Hunter Harvey, Ethan Roberts, Palencia and Thielbar.</p><p>“Injuries add up at some point, right?’’ Counsell said. “And we’ve lost a lot of bodies, and it’s hard when you’ve lost that many bodies, it gets hard to keep replacing them with the same quality, frankly, so the guys have done a great job.</p><p>“They’ve done a heck of a job. And frankly, we’ve got some tired guys right now as well, but they’re doing a heck of a job. And so we have not sacrificed any quality at this point. In my eyes, these guys have pitched great. They’ve done a heck of a job, and it’s one of the reasons why we’ve been able to put together this nice run.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 entries.title: Series against powerhouse Dodgers an important measuring stick for Cubs
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — Across the street from LeBron James’ playground, Crypto.com Arena, there’s a huge ad adorning one side of an entire building. You know the type. Certainly, LeBron does. He has been featured on wall-sized billboards before, in Cleveland, Miami and here.</p><p>But this one doesn’t feature the King. Or his current co-star, Luka Doncic.</p><p>This one, looming imperiously over Olympic Boulevard, features a giant golden baseball, made to look as if it has broken through the wall itself. The ball is framed on top by the unmistakable crisscrossed “LA” logo worn by the Dodgers on their caps. Below, the word “Habit.”</p><p>LA Habit. Any doubt which professional sports team rules the landscape of Southern California?</p><p>“That’s obviously pretty impressive,’’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> shortstop Dansby Swanson said. “I mean, the Dodgers’ brand historically is already one of the top and to just see how they’ve kind of propelled it is a pretty neat thing.</p><p>“Big stadium, obviously a great team to watch. A team of superstars and good personalities and winning baseball and a championship culture. People wonder how to get fans in the seats — have a good team, right?’’</p><p>Four million tickets sold last season, which translates to just under 50,000 fans a night. Back-to-back World Series champs. Five Series appearances in the last nine years, including another title in 2020. Thirteen consecutive seasons of playing in the postseason.</p><p>And in a city which draws its oxygen from its celebrities, the Dodgers have the greatest unicorn of them all, Shohei Ohtani, a global phenomenon unlike any this sport has seen since the Great Bambino himself. One man’s opinion: Ohtani is a better two-way player than Babe Ruth. The Babe all but gave up pitching at 23. Ohtani, who turns 32 on July 5, is 2-0 with an 0.38 ERA in four starts, his last start six shutout innings earlier this week in San Francisco.</p><p>Into this rarefied air come the Cubs and their nine-game winning streak, the longest in the big leagues this season.</p><p>The Dodgers started the night 17-8, tied with the Padres for first place in the NL West and a half-game behind the Braves (18-8) for the majors’ best record.</p><p>The Cubs came in 16-9, tied with the Reds for first in the NL Central.</p><p>The Dodgers had the highest OPS in baseball, .828. The Cubs (.784) were third.</p><p>The Dodgers lead baseball with 42 home runs. The Cubs had 32, tied with the White Sox for fifth place.</p><p>The Cubs have outscored the Dodgers by two runs (139-137). The Cubs have a higher on-base average (.357 to .355). The Dodgers are outslugging the Cubs, .473 to .427. Dodgers pitchers have a 3.27 ERA. The Cubs are at 3.44.</p><p>Two very good baseball teams, taking the measure of each other in April, which may or may not serve as a preview of coming attractions in October.</p><p>“We believe in the group we have,’’ Swanson said about what to make of two heavyweights slugging it out so early on the calendar. “We believe in this team.</p><p>“We believe in putting out a really great product, every night, day or night. So I mean, yes and no [that the Dodgers are a test]. I mean, we want to win. So at the end of the day, we’ve just got to continue to be about our business and our goals. And that doesn’t change depending on who you’re playing, you know? Obviously, it’s fun to be able to play games against them.’’</p><p>And then there is the undercard: In Dodger Blue, outfielder Kyle Tucker, who was paid a lot of money last season by the Cubs to take them deep into October. It didn’t happen.</p><p>The Cubs moved on to Tucker’s former teammate in Houston, third baseman Alex Bregman.</p><p>How different does that make the 2026 Cubs from last year’s team?</p><p>“Obviously,’’ Swanson said, “both players are top players in our league. Very different personalities, but both show up to do their job each and every day.</p><p>“Just like the interactions I’ve had with Breggy — we sort of came up together and played against each other in college — we have a little bit of a unique bond with each other just because of that.</p><p>“But I mean, he fits so seamlessly into our group. entries.title: Munetaka Murakami hits 11th homer in White Sox' win over Nationals
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> general manager Chris Getz heaped seemingly risky praise on Munetaka Murakami when he introduced the Japanese slugger in a news conference at the Rate three days before Christmas.</p><p>Getz raised eyebrows when he called Murakami “one of the most prolific power hitters on the planet.”</p><p>But Getz looks spot-on prophetic. Murakami entered Friday with 10 home runs in 25 games after he tied a Major League Baseball rookie record by homering in five consecutive games — three against the Athletics two against the Diamondbacks — on the White Sox’ just-completed 4-2 road trip.</p><p>Murakami then upped it to 11 homers — and six in his last seven games — with a solo blast to center off Miles Mikolas in the fourth inning of Friday’s series opener against the Nationals at the Rate. That tied a Sox record for 11 drives in March/April of a season set by Paul Konerko in 2010.</p><p>And Murakami, at least temporarily, pulled even with the Astros’ Yordan Alvarez for the major-league home run lead. The Astros slugger also had 11 going into a home game Friday against the Yankees.</p><p>“Well, it was a bold statement and I appreciate him going out there and hitting for power and supporting the statement,” Getz said. “That statement is driven by how much power you know is in that swing, in that body. But we know that it’s easier said than done to go out there and hit for power.</p><p>“And he’s really dialed it in fairly quickly in this league, which you never know until he get the at-bats under his belt. But thankfully for the White Sox, he’s gone out there and performed well.”</p><p>Yep, Murakami has struck out 35 times in his first 109 plate appearance. That was expected after he fanned 25% of the time in eight seasons in Japan. But with the Sox, he was batting .253 with 22 hits and 21 walks, and scored 19 runs in a suddenly productive attack.</p><p>The 26-year-old first baseman’s overall plate presence, not just his power, isn’t lost on Getz.</p><p>“ ‘Mune’ is a prime example of someone that’s punishing, you know, certain pitches in the zone,” Getz said. “But anything outside the zone, he’s taking and earning those walks and other player are exemplifying that as well.</p><p>“He creates plenty of action and the action is either with his bat and when he doesn’t swing and takes walks. That level of patience potentially brings more opportunities for guys that are coming up to the plate with him on base.”</p><p>Getz also saluted Murakami’s work ethic that he called “top of the scale” and extends to defensive work and baserunning.</p><p>Murakami entered Friday tied for second in the majors in homers with 22-year-old Washington slugger James Wood, who had gone deep in three consecutive games.</p><p>First-year Nationals manager Blake Butera has been impressed with Wood — and Murakami — as the two young boppers meet in a potential power show on the South Side this weekend.</p><p>The 6-6, 234-pound Wood, along with shortstop CJ Abrams, are producing big-time for the Nats. Both were acquired from the Padres in August 2022 in the blockbuster deal that sent Juan Soto and Josh Bell to the out west.</p><p>“What ‘Woody’ does really well is he’s able to let the ball travel such a long time,” Butera said. “And with his bat speed — and obviously the size and strength that he has — he can wait just longer to make decisions whether to swing or not.”</p><p>Butera said he had his eye on where Murakami might land in the majors this season.</p><p>“I’ve kind of stayed up to date on how he’s doing,” Butera said. “I know it’s not always easy for Japanese players to come over to the U.S. and jump right into this and have success right away. entries.title: Bears draft LSU WR Zavion Thomas — a Walter Payton relative — No. 89
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> drafted LSU wide receiver Zavion Thomas — who says he's a distant relative of legendary running back Walter Payton — with the 89th pick Friday night.</p><p>The relation is somewhere on the family tree — “It’s still a long way,” Thomas said — but it’s close enough to home for him to appreciate where he was drafted. Thomas grew up hearing stories about Payton. Just minutes after he was drafted by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/24/bears-first-three-picks-in-nfl-draft-nos-25-57-and-69-show-no-urgency-to-attack-biggest-needs" target="_blank" >Bears</a>, Thomas’ grandpa told him he and Payton used to share a bed sometimes when they were kids.</p><p>Joining the Bears in Round 3, then, means a lot. Thomas got a clue that the Bears were interested during a long phone call two weeks ago. The team was attracted to his straight-line speed — he ran a blazing 4.28-second 40-yard dash at the NFL Scouting Combine — as well as his versatility. At LSU, he played outside, in the slot, at running back and returned kicks and punts. He led the SEC in kick return yards two years ago.<br>He even tried throwing a few passes, something that has to intrigue coach Ben Johnson.</p><p>“I’m able to do everything,” he said.</p><p>The 5-foot-10, 190-pound Thomas returned a punt for a touchdown in 2022 and kickoffs for touchdowns in both 2023 and 2024. The 22-year-old started his college career as a punt returner at Mississippi State before transferring to LSU after two years. He had 41 catches for 488 yards last year.</p><p>The Bears’ offensive system is complicated for receivers to learn, general manager Ryan Poles said, so the team is prepared for Thomas to take time to adjust to the NFL. Returning, though, could happen on Day 1.</p><p>“This kid is special with the ball in his hand,” assistant college scouting director Francis St. Paul said. “He has the deep speed to play outside and quickness to play in the slot — and obviously his return ability is what really attracted us.”</p><p>Poles said he wasn’t aware of the Payton connection until after he drafted him.</p><p>“Good genes, right?” he said.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-bc0001" name="list-bc0001"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, items=[{type=Image, anchorId=promo-e50000, _styledTemplate=null, media=[{ampLink=null, _styledTemplate=null, _template=/image/Image.hbs, image={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/58/1baeea4f89758d0c6fa1712b4a56/poles-17.jpg, width=6123, height=4082}, alt=Bears GM Ryan Poles., narrowImage={src=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/a8/58/1baeea4f89758d0c6fa1712b4a56/poles-17.jpg, width=6123, height=4082}}], category=[{items=[Bears]}], imageAlignment=null, isFeatured=false, timestamp=1777082058000, wordCount=879, description=[{items=[After choosing safety Dillon Thieneman in the first round, the Bears went with Iowa center Logan Jones and Stanford tight end Sam Roush in the second. entries.title: Demoted White Sox starter Shane Smith showing improvement in Charlotte
entries.summary: <p>Demoted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> Opening Day starting pitcher <b>Shane Smith</b> was set to make his third Triple-A start on Friday night for the Charlotte Knights as they hosted the Nashville Sounds.</p><p>The 26-year-old Smith has made progress with his mechanics in the minors, general manager<b> Chris Getz</b> said before Friday’s night’s series opener against the Nationals on the South Side. The 6-3 right-hander is 1-0 in two starts covering nine total innings with the Knights so far after struggling in three games with the Sox at the start of the season.</p><p>“We tasked him with some drill work and some areas to focus on with his delivery,” Getz said. “You know, his body changed a little bit in terms of delivery and we just wanted to get him back on track and he’s worked really hard and done pretty well.</p><p>“He’s got a start tonight and we’ll see how tonight goes.”</p><p>Smith became the first rookie pitcher in Sox history to be named an All-Star in 2025, when he went 7-8 with a 3.81 ERA through 29 starts.</p><p>But Smith was pounded in his first two outings of 2026, giving up a combined 12 runs (10 earned) in 4‰ innings. He had a better third start on April 7 against Baltimore, allowing just one hit and no runs in 3‰ innings. He struck out eight, but walked five and hit a batter.</p><h3><b>Teel still healing</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel </b>was in the Sox clubhouse but still isn’t ready to report for a rehab assignment following a Grade 2 right hamstring strain he suffered on March 10. He got hurt running out a double for Team Italy during a win over the U.S. at the World Baseball Classic.</p><p>Teel reportedly was to be sent to Charlotte last Monday, but that was pushed back.</p><p>“We haven’t been able to get it quite to the finish line,” Getz said. “There’s always this final stage and a threshold needs to be met before we send someone else on a rehab.</p><p>“You know we want to be very careful when it comes to Kyle Teel and certainly a hamstring. I know he had a really good day yesterday and he feels good today.”</p><p>Teel, acquired from the Red Sox in the<b> Garrett Crochet</b> trade in December 2024, hit .273 with eight home runs and 35 RBI while walking 37 times in 297 plate appearances in 78 games for the Sox last season.</p><p>“He’s been out for a while now,” Getz added. “You know he missed a chunk of spring training and obviously all of the regular season so far. So I don’t have a finite number of the amount of games [needed in rehab]. You kind of read the situation.”</p><h3><b>Hays, Murphy sent on rehab</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Outfielder <b>Austin Hays </b>and left-handed reliever<b> Chris Murphy </b>are being sent to Charlotte on rehab assignments that start Saturday.</p><p>Hays has been out since sustaining a right hamstring strain on April 6 against the Orioles. Murphy went on the 15-day injured list with left elbow impingement syndrome following a one-inning outing against the Orioles on April 7 when he allowed a run.</p><p>Hays pulled up while pursuing <b>Tyler O’Neill’s</b> fly left in the fourth inning of a 2-1 loss to the Orioles. Manager <b>Will Venable </b>originally said Hays would miss two to four weeks.</p><p>The 30-year-old Hays signed a one-year, $6 million free-agent contract with the Sox in February. He’s batting .219 with a homer and six RBI in nine games.</p><p>Murphy is 1-0 with a 10.50 ERA in six games. He earned his second career save to cap a 3-0 Sox victory over the Blue Jays on April 5 when he pitched a scoreless ninth — and fielded a popup himself.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: Bears' first three picks in NFL Draft — Nos. 25, 57 and 69 — show no urgency to attack biggest needs
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ first three picks in the draft seemed to be geared more toward their future than their present. For a team aspiring to make the leap from good to great in the upcoming season, where was general manager Ryan Poles’ urgency to address red flags at left tackle, defensive tackle and defensive end?</p><p>There’s nothing wrong or crazy about what they did in the first three rounds of the NFL Draft, but they didn’t aggressively attack their three biggest needs.</p><p>The Bears went into the week with concerns at left tackle, defensive tackle and defensive end, and that’s still the case Friday night. They chose Iowa center Logan Jones on Friday in the second round at No. 57 overall, then took Stanford tight end Sam Roush in the third at No. 69 overall after trading out of the 60th pick to add a fifth-round pick at No. 144 overall.</p><p>In the first round Thursday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/24/dillon-thieneman-got-to-the-nfl-by-using-criticism-to-improve-thatll-serve-him-well-with-the-bears" >the Bears used the No. 25 pick on safety Dillion Thieneman</a>.</p><p>That essentially means three problems remain status quo:</p><p>- There will be a wide-ranging open competition for the starting left tackle job, just like last summer.</p><p>- A pass rush that has ranked second-to-last in the NFL over the Poles era is still riding on Montez Sweat and several unproven candidates to be his running mate.</p><p>- One of the NFL’s worst run defenses from last season likely will have the same two starting defensive tackles in Gervon Dexter and Grady Jarrett.</p><p>Poles has said he believes some improvement will come from within, but that’s more on faith than on concrete evidence.</p><p>At defensive end, Sweat has been good, but made just one Pro Bowl in his first three seasons. The others, most notably Dayo Odeyingbo and Austin Booker, have never had more than eight sacks in a season. And the Bears haven’t seen enough from 2025 second-round pick Shemar Turner to know if he’ll be a force.</p><p>Similarly to Sweat, Dexter has been solid, but not overwhelming, and Jarrett has dealt with injuries over the last few seasons and is approaching his 33rd birthday.</p><p>The starting left tackle is anybody’s guess.</p><p>Braxton Jones appears to be the leader at this stage, but he won the job at the end of training camp last year only to lose it by Week 4. Theo Benedet, also eventually benched, is another candidate. Kiran Amegadjie has played just six games since Poles drafted him No. 75 overall in 2024 and will have a tough road to make this roster. They signed Jedrick Wills, the former No. 10 overall pick, but he hasn’t played since November 2024.</p><p>Their fastest path to being a contender is to propel quarterback Caleb Williams forward. Sending him into the season without a good plan at left tackle isn’t helping.</p><p>And if skipping those positions with the Nos. 25 and 57 overall picks, it was outright laughable with the No. 69 pick. Nothing against Roush, but that was a weird choice given their roster. The Bears drafted tight end Colston Loveland 10th overall last year and still have veteran Cole Kmet under contract for two more seasons.</p><p>The Bears traded a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Patriots for Garrett Bradbury in March as Poles saw the market for centers surging ahead of Tyler Linderbaum getting a three-year, $81 million deal from the Raiders. This is Bradbury’s third team in three seasons, though, and he was unlikely to be a long-term solution.</p><p>Bradbury will be an asset to Jones, who can take as long as he needs to acclimate and learn coach Ben Johnson’s offense. Bradbury likely will be the Bears’ Week 1 starter, providing Jones some margin.</p><p>Jones, 24, actually began his collegiate career as a defensive tackle and switched to offense when Linderbaum left Iowa for the NFL.</p><p>“I haven’t even played my best football yet and I haven’t figured [center] out,” he said despite winning the Rimington Trophy as the best center in college football. “It’s been a journey, but the past two years, for sure, is when I realized that if I really wanted this, I’ve just got to go out there and take it.”</p><p>While the plan for Jones likely will be to develop behind Bradbury until he’s ready, it’s hard to see where exactly Roush fits.</p><p>Roush, 22, had his best season at Stanford last year with 49 catches for 545 yards and two touchdowns. With the Bears, though, Loveland figures to be a focal point, if not the centerpiece, of the passing attack, and the Bears just restructured Kmet’s contract to lower his salary-cap number for this season by kicking money into 2027.</p><p>Poles said in February he felt “pretty good” about Kmet staying with the team this season, and Kmet said this week that Poles and Johnson made clear he has value to them, but the phones might start lighting up with inquiries about Kmet.</p><p>All three of the players the Bears took in the first two rounds — Thieneman, Jones and Roush — are highly rated prospects who could turn out to be excellent pros. Thieneman in particular seems to have all the makings of a star.</p><p>But having a great safety, center and an extra tight end aren’t going to help the Bears as much as fortifying their pass rush, run defense and protection of Williams would have — especially if their expectations truly are to win now.</p>

entries.title: Person struck, killed while riding scooter in Douglas
entries.summary: <p>A person died after being hit by a car while riding a scooter in the Douglas neighborhood Friday, police said.</p><p>The unidentified woman was riding a scooter around 4:15 p.m. in the 3300 block of South King Drive when she was struck by a Jeep, police said. The woman was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead.</p><p>Chicago police didn't provide an exact age, nor did they say if she was an adult or a minor.</p><p>The driver of the Jeep, a 36-year-old woman, was cited for failure to avoid an accident.</p><p>Chicago police major accidents unit is investigating.</p><p>The crash comes one month after 15-year-old Violet Harris was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/03/22/girl-15-killed-while-riding-scooter-in-south-shore-hit-and-run" >killed in a hit-and-run</a> in South Shore. Traumas related to e-scooters have<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2024/10/09/lime-divvy-chicago-e-scooter-riders-serious-injuries" > increased in Chicago in recent years</a>.</p>

entries.title: Pope Leo affirms support for banning death penalty, marks 15 years since Illinois ban
entries.summary: <p>Pope Leo XIV emphasized his support for banning the death penalty in a video sent Friday to DePaul University students.</p><p>“We affirm that the dignity of the person is not lost even after very serious crimes are committed,” the pope said in a two-minute video.</p><p>The message was sent to mark 15 years since Illinois abolished the death penalty — and on the same day the Trump Administration announced a new death penalty push.</p><p>“Effective systems of detention can be and have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption,” Pope Leo said.</p><p>“This is why Pope Francis and my recent predecessors repeatedly insisted that the common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment,” he continued. “Consequently, the church teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.”</p><p>The video was played for about 250 DePaul students, faculty and staff at a celebration honoring the 15th anniversary of Illinois abolishing the death penalty. Former Gov. Pat Quinn, who in 2011 signed the legislation to ban capital punishment in Illinois, also attended.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/TMbh1veDrvQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Pope Leo XIV Supports U.S. Efforts to Abolish the Death Penalty"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Former Gov. George Ryan started the process to end the death penalty in Illinois in 2000, when he issued a moratorium on executions and said the system needed to be investigated.</p><p>Ryan emptied the state’s death row three years later by commuting the sentences of 167 death row inmates to life in prison and pardoning four inmates.</p><p>“I have had mixed emotions concerning this issue,” Ryan told the Sun-Times in 2003 after he commuted the sentences.</p><p>“I thought about it night and day. I finally came to the conclusion that this was the right decision and I'm going to have to live with it,” Ryan said. “Maybe [Saturday] morning I'll wake up and be uncomfortable with my decision. But I will live with it no matter what. I believe it's the right thing to do."</p><p>Twelve people, including mass murderer John Wayne Gacy, were executed by Illinois between the time it was re-imposed in 1977, and 1999. Ryan's moratorium took effect the next year.</p><p>Ryan, who died last year, later was sentenced to 6 ½ years in prison for unrelated corruption charges.</p><p>His moratorium on the death penalty continued while two Illinois commissions studied the use of capital punishment for serious crimes.</p><p>When then-Gov. Quinn <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilsos.gov/departments/archives/online-exhibits/100-documents/2011-death-penalty-abolished.html" target="_blank" >signed the legislation banning the death penalty</a>, Illinois became the 16th state to do so. That legislation sat on his desk for weeks while Quinn pondered his decision and was lobbied by many people on both sides, including Cardinal Francis George, who urged him to sign it, the Sun-Times reported at the time.</p><p>In his Friday video, Pope Leo praised "the decision made by the governor of Illinois in 2011," to sign that legislation.</p><p>"I likewise offer my support to those who advocate for the abolition of the death penalty in the United States of America and around the world," the pope continued. "I pray that your efforts will lead to a greater acknowledgment of the dignity of every person and will inspire others to work for the same just cause."</p><p>Also on Friday, the Trump Administration announced changes in death penalty policy, the Associated Press reported. </p><p>The Justice Department will adopt firing squads as a permitted method of execution, officials said Friday. The department also is reauthorizing the use of single-drug lethal injections with pentobarbital, which was used to carry out 13 executions during the first Trump administration — more than under any president in modern history. The Biden administration had removed pentobarbital from the federal protocol over concerns about the potential for unnecessary pain and suffering.<br></p>

entries.title: NFL Draft: Bears trade back from Pick 60, take Stanford TE Sam Roush
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> traded away their No. 60 overall pick in the second round Friday, getting a third- and fifth-round pick from the Titans for their troubles. The Bears picked Stanford tight end Sam Roush No. 69 and hold Pick 144 Saturday afternoon.</p><p>Roush caught 49 balls for 545 yards last year and was named second-team All-ACC. He joins last year's first-round pick, Colston Loveland, and veteran Cole Kmet. Bears coach Ben Johnson is among the NFL's leaders in using multiple tight end sets. Johnson ran "13" personnel, which uses three tight ends, on 8.5 percent of the Bears' downs last year.</p><p>"If you ask coach (Ben Johnson), it's the more, the merrier ..." player personnel director Trey Koziol said. "In the tight end room, we can play all those guys."</p><p>Roush has experience at both the in-line position as a catching threat, Koziol said.</p><p>The Stanford alum said the Bears have an "incredible tight end room," saying "there's a lot I can learn from them." He's already familiar with tight end Jim Dray, who played collegiately at Stanford.</p><p>Roush said he's prepared to play special teams and help with run-blocking as a rookie. Football is in his blood. His great-uncle is Pro Football Hall of Famer Merlin Olsen. His maternal grandfather, Phil, who is the late Merlin's brother and also a former NFL player, was with him Friday night.</p><p>The Atlanta-born Roush moved around the world, living in Asia, with his father's business before settling in San Jose, California, where he played high school football. He holds a Stanford degree and is working on a Master's in computer science.</p><p>The Bears held Pick 60 after dealing receiver DJ Moore to the Bills. By moving back, the Bears filled a gap that existed before the draft began. They weren't scheduled to have picks in either Round 5 or Round 6 until making the move Friday night.</p><p>Three picks before they made the trade, the Bears picked Iowa center Logan Jones No. 57 overall.</p><p>Bears general manager Ryan Poles is known to trade back on the second and third day of the draft to collect picks. He's in his fifth draft and has only made one prominent move up on draft day, trading for cornerback Tyrique Stevenson.</p><p>The Bears made Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman their first-round pick Thursday night. They picked Iowa center <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/04/24/bears-nfl-draft-logan-jones-57-second-round-pick-center-drew-dalman-garrett-bradbury" target="_blank" >Logan entries.title: NFL Draft: Bears take Iowa center Logan Jones No. 57
entries.summary: <p>Less than two months after starting center Drew Dalman abruptly announced his retirement, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" >Bears</a> used their first of two second-round picks on his long-term replacement, drafting Iowa’s Logan Jones with the No. 57 pick.</p><p>Jones won the Rimington Trophy last year, which is given to the best center in college football.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/03/03/bears-drew-dalman-expected-to-retire-center-ryan-poles-falcons-stanford-nfl" >When Dalman retired,</a> the Bears quickly pivoted and traded a 2027 fifth-round pick for the Patriots’ Garrett Bradbury. He’s entering the final year of his contract, though, and the Bears couldn’t pass on the chance to add a player from one of the premier offensive lineman development programs in America. Bradbury and the 6-foot-2, 299-pound Jones figure to compete for the starting center job during training camp.</p><p>"It's adding competition to the room," player personnel director Trey Koziol said.</p><p>General manager Ryan Poles said that the Bears are comfortable with Bradbury as the starter and are happy to have Jones develop behind him to begin the season.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson "likes to put a lot on the center’s plate, which is awesome," Jones said. Jones visited Halas Hall as part of a pre-draft visit.</p><p>"Playing center, it’s your job to get everybody into order and know what they’re doing," he said. "Whether it be a combo [block], a pass-pro[tection], whatever it might be -- they put a lot on the center. It’s definitely going to be challenging. But I look forward to it. It’s definitely going to be a lot of fun, for sure.”</p><p>Koziol said the Bears liked Jones' "mental stamina" as well as his intensity and physicality.</p><p>The Council Bluffs -born center was a team captain last year. He won state tiles in the shot put and discus in high school and went to Iowa as a defensive lineman. He moved to center and took over for Tyler Linderbaum, who was drafted by the Ravens and was just made the richest center in NFL history by the Raiders.</p><p>As part of a promotion, Jones will receive a lifetime's worth of ketchup from Kraft-Heinz because he was the No. 57 pick.</p><p>The Bears entered Friday night with three Day 2 picks, starting with No. 57 overall. They used their first-round pick, No. 25, on Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman on Thursday night.</p><p>The Bears still have needs at edge rusher, defensive tackle, cornerback, offensive tackle and even entries.title: New Trier quarterback Jackie Ryder commits to Purdue
entries.summary: <p>New Trier’s Jackie Ryder was playing wide receiver in middle school when his dad Brian — a former tight end at Arizona State — had an idea that changed the trajectory of his son’s career.</p><p>“It was my dad who wanted me to switch [to quarterback],” Ryder told the Sun-Times. “I always had a good arm, was a good athlete. It wasn’t very hard.”</p><p>And now the three-star prospect is a Big Ten recruit. Ryder, who is No. 35 in Illinois’ 2027 recruiting cycle according to the 247Sports composite rankings, committed to Purdue earlier this month.</p><p>The Boilermakers, who are rebuilding under second-year coach Barry Odom, have been in contact with Ryder for more than a year.</p><p>“They really wanted me,” said Ryder, who also had Group of Five offers from North Texas and Southern Mississippi as well as interest from other mid-majors.</p><p>But the chance to play in a Power Four league close to home was impossible to resist.</p><p>“Originally I thought I would figure out [a college choice] in June,” Ryder said. “But I felt this was the right opportunity.”</p><p>He believes Odom can right the ship at Purdue the same way he did in his previous stop at UNLV.</p><p>“I just love his vision for the program, getting back to how Purdue was back in the day,” Ryder said. “I see him going to work for me and the rest of the program.”</p><p>Ryder has been a late bloomer, according to Trevians coach Brian Doll.</p><p>“Jackie is a kid who probably developed six months later than some other kids,” Doll said. “He has put on some pretty good weight.”</p><p>Ryder now carries 220 pounds on his 6-5 frame, up from 185 a year ago.</p><p>“His body has just really developed,” Doll said. “He looks the part.”</p><p>Ryder had a productive junior season as New Trier went 5-5 and reached the Class 8A playoffs. He completed 55% of his passes for 1,784 yards and 17 touchdowns with four interceptions. Ryder isn’t a dual-threat quarterback, but he was an effective runner in a small sample size with 19 carries for 163 yards and four touchdowns.</p><p>“He’s kind of sneaky agile and quick for a kid his size,” Doll said.</p><p>Ryder’s calling card is his big arm. “He’s able to push the ball downfield, [throw] the deep outs,” Doll said.</p><p>Ryder also is a standout pitcher/outfielder for New Trier’s baseball team. But his future is in football, and he breaks a long drought<br>for the Trevians. Doll believes Ryder is the first Big Ten quarterback the program has produced since Rich Weiss played at Illinois in the late 1970s.</p><p>While some elite athletes specialize in their primary sport as their prep careers wind down, Ryder had no thought of giving up baseball.</p><p>“It’s pretty hectic but I’m really enjoying it,” he said of juggling both sports.</p><p>With a promising group of receivers that includes another two-sport standout — sophomore lacrosse star Ben Sullivan — Ryder is upbeat about the Trevians’ prospects this fall.</p><p>“We’ve got a lot of guys coming up I feel strong about,” he said.</p><p>Just like he feels strongly about heading to West Lafayette, Indiana, down the road.<br></p>
